subject: St Polycarp of Smyrna

text_used.text: Quotations are word for word from public-domain translations, fetched as plain text into design/saints-hub/sources/people/polycarp-of-smyrna/. The main text is the Roberts-Donaldson translation in the Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), CCEL plain text (anf01.txt), because it is clean text and the Irenaeus page already uses it. Lightfoot's translation (The Apostolic Fathers, Part II, vol. 3, 1889; reprinted 1891) is used where its wording is the famous one ('Be strong, Polycarp, and play the man'; 'Fourscore and six years'); it is checked against the archive.org OCR of the 1889 volume with only end-of-line hyphens joined. The Greek is Kirsopp Lake's text (Loeb, 1913), as corrected and encoded by the Open Greek and Latin First1KGreek project. Eusebius and McGiffert's notes: NPNF 2nd series vol. 1 (1890), CCEL. Jerome: Richardson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 3 (1892), CCEL. Tertullian: ANF vol. 3, CCEL. 'exact' is the edition's wording; 'display' applies the site's capitals for every pronoun for God, nothing else. Every exact and every evidence snippet below was found by script in the named file (build_words.py in the session scratchpad; same normalisation as verify-quotes.mjs).
text_used.note: CAUTION: the Lightfoot text on earlychristianwritings.com is marked 'Adapt. and mod. (c) 1990 ATHENA DATA PRODUCTS' and is NOT Lightfoot's 1889/1891 wording in every line: do not quote it (ecw-martyrdompolycarp-lightfoot.txt, ecw-polycarp-lightfoot.txt kept only for reference). The ECW Kirsopp Lake pages are Lake's 1912-13 Loeb text. CCEL chapter URL pattern: Martyrdom anf01.iv.iv.<roman chapter>, Letter anf01.iv.ii.<roman chapter>, Ignatius to Polycarp anf01.v.viii.<roman>, Against Heresies Book 3 chapter 3 anf01.ix.iv.iv; each was fetched (HTTP 200) and holds the named chapter.

feature.text: Eighty and six years have I served Him, and He never did me any injury: how then can I blaspheme my King and my Saviour?

feature.exact: Eighty and six years have I served Him, and He never did me any injury: how then can I blaspheme my King and my Saviour?
feature.source: Martyrdom of Polycarp (the letter of the church at Smyrna), chapter 9, tr. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885)
feature.note: Roberts-Donaldson wording (ANF 1). His answer when the proconsul said 'Swear, and I will set thee at liberty, reproach Christ.' Capitals already as printed.

feature.text: Fourscore and six years have I been His servant, and He hath done me no wrong. How then can I blaspheme my King Who saved me?
feature.display: Fourscore and six years have I been His servant, and He hath done me no wrong. How then can I blaspheme my King Who saved me?
feature.exact: Fourscore and six years have I been His servant, and He hath done me no wrong. How then can I blaspheme my King who saved me?
feature.source: Martyrdom of Polycarp, chapter 9, tr. J. B. Lightfoot, The Apostolic Fathers, Part II, vol. 3 (2nd ed. 1889), p. 481 (the same translation is reprinted in Lightfoot and Harmer, 1891)
feature.note: Lightfoot's wording, the one most quoted online ('my King who saved me' is closer to the Greek 'τὸν σώσαντά με'). Either translation may lead; do not mix them in one line.

feature.text: Ὀγδοήκοντα καὶ ἓξ ἔτη δουλεύω αὐτῷ, καὶ οὐδέν με ἠδίκησεν: καὶ πῶς δύναμαι βλασφημῆσαι τὸν βασιλέα μου τὸν σώσαντά με;
feature.display: Ὀγδοήκοντα καὶ ἓξ ἔτη δουλεύω αὐτῷ, καὶ οὐδέν με ἠδίκησεν: καὶ πῶς δύναμαι βλασφημῆσαι τὸν βασιλέα μου τὸν σώσαντά με;
feature.exact: Ὀγδοήκοντα καὶ ἓξ ἔτη δουλεύω αὐτῷ, καὶ οὐδέν με ἠδίκησεν: καὶ πῶς δύναμαι βλασφημῆσαι τὸν βασιλέα μου τὸν σώσαντά με;
feature.source: Martyrium Polycarpi 9.3, Greek text of Kirsopp Lake, The Apostolic Fathers vol. 2 (Loeb, 1913; the digital text is from the 1917 printing), encoded by First1KGreek (Perseus / Open Greek and Latin). The printed page: https://archive.org/details/apostolicfathers02lakeuoft (p. 324).
feature.note: The digital text writes the Greek raised stop (ano teleia) as a colon; in print it is 'ἠδίκησεν·'. For display use: 'Ὀγδοήκοντα καὶ ἓξ ἔτη δουλεύω αὐτῷ, καὶ οὐδέν με ἠδίκησεν· καὶ πῶς δύναμαι βλασφημῆσαι τὸν βασιλέα μου τὸν σώσαντά με;'. 'δουλεύω' is present tense and means to serve as a slave serves: literally 'eighty and six years I am slaving for Him'. Greek pronouns for God are left as the edition prints them (the capitals rule is for English).

words.display: I must be burnt alive.
words.exact: I must be burnt alive.
words.source: Martyrdom of Polycarp (the letter of the church at Smyrna), chapter 5, tr. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885)
words.note: Three days before his arrest, praying at a farm outside the city, he saw his pillow on fire, and turned to those with him. Repeated in chapter 12 when the crowd calls for fire.

words.note: When the police found him in the upper room of a cottage. He could have slipped away to another place and would not. ANF's footnote: some manuscripts read 'the will of the Lord'.

words.display: I shall not do as you advise me.
words.exact: I shall not do as you advise me.
words.source: Martyrdom of Polycarp (the letter of the church at Smyrna), chapter 8, tr. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885)
words.note: To Herod the police captain and his father Nicetes, who took him into their carriage and asked, 'What harm is there in saying, Lord Caesar, and in sacrificing ... and so make sure of safety?'

words.text: Away with the Atheists.
words.display: Away with the Atheists.
words.exact: Away with the Atheists.
words.source: Martyrdom of Polycarp (the letter of the church at Smyrna), chapter 9, tr. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885)
words.note: The proconsul told him to say it, meaning the Christians. Polycarp looked at the crowd, waved his hand at them, groaned, looked up to heaven, and said it of them. ANF note: 'Referring the words to the heathen, and not to the Christians, as was desired.'

words.text: Since thou art vainly urgent that, as thou sayest, I should swear by the fortune of Cæsar, and pretendest not to know who and what I am, hear me declare with boldness, I am a Christian.
words.display: Since thou art vainly urgent that, as thou sayest, I should swear by the fortune of Cæsar, and pretendest not to know who and what I am, hear me declare with boldness, I am a Christian.
words.exact: Since thou art vainly urgent that, as thou sayest, I should swear by the fortune of Cæsar, and pretendest not to know who and what I am, hear me declare with boldness, I am a Christian.
words.source: Martyrdom of Polycarp (the letter of the church at Smyrna), chapter 10, tr. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885)
words.note: When pressed a third time to swear by Caesar's fortune (Lightfoot: 'genius'). The short form 'Hear me declare with boldness, I am a Christian' is what quote sites carry; it is genuine.

words.text: And if you wish to learn what the doctrines of Christianity are, appoint me a day, and thou shalt hear them.
words.display: And if you wish to learn what the doctrines of Christianity are, appoint me a day, and thou shalt hear them.
words.exact: And if you wish to learn what the doctrines of Christianity are, appoint me a day, and thou shalt hear them.
words.source: Martyrdom of Polycarp (the letter of the church at Smyrna), chapter 10, tr. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885)
words.note: He offers the proconsul a day's hearing on the faith. The proconsul answers, 'Persuade the people.'

words.text: To thee I have thought it right to offer an account [of my faith]; for we are taught to give all due honour (which entails no injury upon ourselves) to the powers and authorities which are ordained of God. But as for these, I do not deem them worthy of receiving any account from me.
words.display: To thee I have thought it right to offer an account [of my faith]; for we are taught to give all due honour (which entails no injury upon ourselves) to the powers and authorities which are ordained of God. But as for these, I do not deem them worthy of receiving any account from me.

words.source: Martyrdom of Polycarp (the letter of the church at Smyrna), chapter 10, tr. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885)
words.note: He will explain himself to the governor, whom God set in office (Romans 13), but not to a mob. McGiffert (note 1150): he 'preferred to retain his dignity and not compromise himself by appearing to ask for mercy'.

words.text: Call them then, for we are not accustomed to repent of what is good in order to adopt that which is evil; and it is well for me to be changed from what is evil to what is righteous.
words.display: Call them then, for we are not accustomed to repent of what is good in order to adopt that which is evil; and it is well for me to be changed from what is evil to what is righteous.
words.exact: Call them then, for we are not accustomed to repent of what is good in order to adopt that which is evil; and it is well for me to be changed from what is evil to what is righteous.
words.source: Martyrdom of Polycarp (the letter of the church at Smyrna), chapter 11, tr. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885)
words.note: To 'I have wild beasts at hand; to these will I cast thee, except thou repent.' A play on the proconsul's word 'repent'. Lightfoot's version: 'the repentance from better to worse is a change not permitted to us'.

words.text: Thou threatenest me with fire which burneth for an hour, and after a little is extinguished, but art ignorant of the fire of the coming judgment and of eternal punishment, reserved for the ungodly. But why tarriest thou? Bring forth what thou wilt.
words.display: Thou threatenest me with fire which burneth for an hour, and after a little is extinguished, but art ignorant of the fire of the coming judgment and of eternal punishment, reserved for the ungodly. But why tarriest thou? Bring forth what thou wilt.

words.source: Martyrdom of Polycarp (the letter of the church at Smyrna), chapter 11, tr. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885)
words.note: To the threat of fire. Quote sites carry a modern form: 'But why do you delay? Come, do what you will.'

words.text: Leave me as I am; for He that giveth me strength to endure the fire, will also enable me, without your securing me by nails, to remain without moving in the pile.
words.display: Leave me as I am; for He that giveth me strength to endure the fire, will also enable me, without your securing me by nails, to remain without moving in the pile.
words.exact: Leave me as I am; for He that giveth me strength to endure the fire, will also enable me, without your securing me by nails, to remain without moving in the pile.
words.source: Martyrdom of Polycarp (the letter of the church at Smyrna), chapter 13, tr. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885)
words.note: When they were about to nail him to the stake. 'They did not nail him then, but simply bound him' (chapter 14).

words.text: I do know thee, the first-born of Satan.
words.display: I do know thee, the first-born of Satan.
words.exact: I do know thee, the first-born of Satan.
words.source: Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book 3, chapter 3, part 4, tr. A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, ANF vol. 1 (1885)
words.note: Marcion met him once and asked, 'Dost thou know me?' Irenaeus tells it as a sign of 'the horror which the apostles and their disciples had against holding even verbal communication with any corrupters of the truth'. Eusebius's version (Church History 4.14): 'Knowest thou us?' ... 'I know the first born of Satan.' The same phrase is in his own Letter, chapter 7.

words.text: O good God, unto what times hast Thou spared me that I should endure these things?
words.display: O good God, unto what times hast Thou spared me that I should endure these things?
words.exact: O good God, unto what times hast thou spared me that I should endure these things?
words.source: Eusebius, Church History, Book 5, chapter 20, tr. A. C. McGiffert, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 1 (1890), quoting Irenaeus's letter to Florinus
words.note: Irenaeus says this was his usual cry ('as was his custom') when he heard false teaching, and that he 'would have cried out, and stopped his ears' and fled the place. Already on the Irenaeus page (quotes file) with the same display.

words.text: For neither I, nor any other such one, can come up to the wisdom of the blessed and glorified Paul.
words.display: For neither I, nor any other such one, can come up to the wisdom of the blessed and glorified Paul.
words.exact: For neither I, nor any other such one, can come up to the wisdom of the blessed and glorified Paul.
words.source: Polycarp, Letter to the Philippians, chapter 3, tr. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885)
words.note: The Philippians had asked him to write about righteousness. He says he writes only because they asked, and points them to Paul's own letter to them.

words.text: For if any one be inwardly possessed of these graces, he hath fulfilled the command of righteousness, since he that hath love is far from all sin.

words.note: Faith, 'followed by hope, and preceded by love towards God, and Christ, and our neighbour'.

words.exact: But He who raised Him up from the dead will raise up us also, if we do His will, and walk in His commandments, and love what He loved

words.note: The sentence goes on with a list of what to keep from: unrighteousness, covetousness, love of money, evil speaking, false witness.

words.note: He quotes Ephesians 2:8-9. Often cited in debates on grace and works. The inner marks are the edition's; the checker compares straight quotes.

words.display: not quickly crediting [an evil report] against any one, not severe in judgment, as knowing that we are all under a debt of sin.
words.exact: not quickly crediting [an evil report] against any one, not severe in judgment, as knowing that we are all under a debt of sin.

words.note: What he asks of presbyters (elders): 'compassionate and merciful to all, bringing back those that wander, visiting all the sick, and not neglecting the widow, the orphan, or the poor'.

words.text: If then we entreat the Lord to forgive us, we ought also ourselves to forgive
words.display: If then we entreat the Lord to forgive us, we ought also ourselves to forgive
words.exact: If then we entreat the Lord to forgive us, we ought also ourselves to forgive
words.source: Polycarp, Letter to the Philippians, chapter 6, tr. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885)
words.note: Same chapter, same elders.

words.text: whosoever perverts the oracles of the Lord to his own lusts, and says that there is neither a resurrection nor a judgment, he is the first-born of Satan.
words.display: whosoever perverts the oracles of the Lord to his own lusts, and says that there is neither a resurrection nor a judgment, he is the first-born of Satan.
words.exact: whosoever perverts the oracles of the Lord to his own lusts, and says that there is neither a resurrection nor a judgment, he is the first-born of Satan.
words.source: Polycarp, Letter to the Philippians, chapter 7, tr. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885)
words.note: The chapter opens with 1 John 4:3 ('whosoever does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, is antichrist'). The words he later used to Marcion's face.

words.text: let us return to the word which has been handed down to us from the beginning
words.display: let us return to the word which has been handed down to us from the beginning
words.exact: let us return to the word which has been handed down to us from the beginning

words.note: Quote sites carry a modern form: 'Let us, therefore, forsake the vanity of the crowd and their false teachings, and turn back to the word delivered to us from the beginning.' The sense is genuine.

words.text: Let us then be imitators of His patience; and if we suffer for His name's sake, let us glorify Him.

words.exact: Let us then be imitators of His patience; and if we suffer for His name's sake, let us glorify Him.
words.source: Polycarp, Letter to the Philippians, chapter 8, tr. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885)
words.note: Written years before his own martyrdom.

words.text: For they loved not this present world, but Him Who died for us, and for our sakes was raised again by God from the dead.

words.note: Of Ignatius, Zosimus, Rufus, Paul and the other apostles: the martyrs the Philippians had seen.

words.text: Stand fast, therefore, in these things, and follow the example of the Lord, being firm and unchangeable in the faith, loving the brotherhood, and being attached to one another, joined together in the truth, exhibiting the meekness of the Lord in your intercourse with one another, and despising no one.

words.text: When you can do good, defer it not
words.display: When you can do good, defer it not
words.exact: When you can do good, defer it not
words.source: Polycarp, Letter to the Philippians, chapter 10, tr. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885)
words.note: Followed by 'because "alms delivers from death"' (Tobit 4:10): a line from a deuterocanonical book, quoted as Scripture.

words.text: If a man does not keep himself from covetousness, he shall be defiled by idolatry, and shall be judged as one of the heathen.
words.display: If a man does not keep himself from covetousness, he shall be defiled by idolatry, and shall be judged as one of the heathen.
words.exact: If a man does not keep himself from covetousness, he shall be defiled by idolatry, and shall be judged as one of the heathen.
words.source: Polycarp, Letter to the Philippians, chapter 11, tr. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885)
words.note: About Valens, a presbyter at Philippi who fell into (it seems) a money scandal.

words.text: I am deeply grieved, therefore, brethren, for him (Valens) and his wife; to whom may the Lord grant true repentance!
words.display: I am deeply grieved, therefore, brethren, for him (Valens) and his wife; to whom may the Lord grant true repentance!
words.exact: I am deeply grieved, therefore, brethren, for him (Valens) and his wife; to whom may the Lord grant true repentance!
words.source: Polycarp, Letter to the Philippians, chapter 11, tr. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885)
words.note: The line that shows the man: grief, not scorn, for a fallen elder.

words.text: but call them back as suffering and straying members, that ye may save your whole body.
words.display: but call them back as suffering and straying members, that ye may save your whole body.
words.exact: but call them back as suffering and straying members, that ye may save your whole body.
words.source: Polycarp, Letter to the Philippians, chapter 11, tr. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885)
words.note: The sentence begins: 'And be ye then moderate in regard to this matter, and "do not count such as enemies,"' (2 Thessalonians 3:15).

words.text: For I trust that ye are well versed in the Sacred Scriptures, and that nothing is hid from you; but to me this privilege is not yet granted.
words.display: For I trust that ye are well versed in the Sacred Scriptures, and that nothing is hid from you; but to me this privilege is not yet granted.
words.exact: For I trust that ye are well versed in the Sacred Scriptures, and that nothing is hid from you; but to me this privilege is not yet granted.
words.source: Polycarp, Letter to the Philippians, chapter 12, tr. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885)
words.note: A surprising modesty from a man whose letter is woven almost entirely from Scripture. ANF note 404: 'This passage is very obscure'; some render 'it is not granted unto me to practise that which is written'.

words.text: The Epistles of Ignatius written by him to us, and all the rest [of his Epistles] which we have by us, we have sent to you, as you requested.
words.display: The Epistles of Ignatius written by him to us, and all the rest [of his Epistles] which we have by us, we have sent to you, as you requested.
words.exact: The Epistles of Ignatius written by him to us, and all the rest [of his Epistles] which we have by us, we have sent to you, as you requested.
words.source: Polycarp, Letter to the Philippians, chapter 13, tr. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885)
words.note: Why Ignatius's letters survive: Polycarp collected them and sent them on. Chapter 13 was once argued to be added; McGiffert (Eusebius 4.14, note 1127) calls its rejection 'quite arbitrary'.

prayers.text: O Lord God Almighty, the Father of Thy beloved and blessed Son Jesus Christ, by Whom we have received the knowledge of Thee, the God of angels and powers, and of every creature, and of the whole race of the righteous who live before Thee, I give Thee thanks that Thou hast counted me worthy of this day and this hour, that I should have a part in the number of Thy martyrs, in the cup of Thy Christ, to the resurrection of eternal life, both of soul and body, through the incorruption [imparted] by the Holy Ghost. Among whom may I be accepted this day before Thee as a fat and acceptable sacrifice, according as Thou, the ever-truthful God, hast foreordained, hast revealed beforehand to me, and now hast fulfilled. Wherefore also I praise Thee for all things, I bless Thee, I glorify Thee, along with the everlasting and heavenly Jesus Christ, Thy beloved Son, with Whom, to Thee, and the Holy Ghost, be glory both now and to all coming ages. Amen.

prayers.note: Bound to the stake, hands behind him, 'like a distinguished ram [taken] out of a great flock for sacrifice'. The whole prayer. myths.text: Probably true, but it is not what he said. His words count years of serving Christ: “Eighty and six years have I served Him”. Most scholars since Lightfoot read it as his age, so born about 69 or 70. Others count from his baptism. Eusebius's translator McGiffert: “we cannot tell.”
myths.source: Martyrdom of Polycarp, chapter 9; J. B. Lightfoot, The Apostolic Fathers, Part II, vol. 1 (1889), pp. 437-438; McGiffert's note 1147 on Eusebius, Church History 4.15; Kirsopp Lake (1913), note on chapter 9
myths.note: Lightfoot: 'the former would be the more natural interpretation' and 'he must have been born about the year 69 or 70'. Lake's footnote: 'He was therefore probably a Christian born, unless we ascribe to him a quite improbable age.' Halloix and Ussher read it as years of Christian life. Many pages (even the scholarly 'Judaism and Rome' site: 'the eighty-six-year-old bishop') state the age as fact.
evidence: Whether the eighty-six years are to be reckoned from Polycarp's birth, or from the time of his conversion or baptism, we cannot tell.

myths.claim: “The apostle John made him bishop of Smyrna.”
myths.text: The earliest witness says “apostles”, not John by name. Irenaeus, who knew him, wrote that he was “by apostles in Asia, appointed bishop”. Tertullian, about 200, says the church of Smyrna “records that Polycarp was placed therein by John”. Jerome says the same. The fourth-century Life says the neighbouring bishops consecrated him, after Bucolus.
myths.source: Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book 3, chapter 3; Tertullian, Prescription against Heretics, chapter 32; Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 17; the Life of Polycarp ascribed to Pionius, chapter 23
myths.note: McGiffert (note 1116) thinks Irenaeus's 'appointed by apostles' may be his own inference: 'probably to be looked upon as a combination of his own'. Lightfoot notes the Pionian Life 'says not a word' of John. The 1916 Roman Martyrology: 'a disciple of the Apostle St. John, who consecrated him bishop'. So: the John tradition is early (Tertullian) but not in Irenaeus's words.
evidence: was also, by apostles in Asia, appointed bishop of the Church in Smyrna
the church of Smyrna, which records that Polycarp was placed therein by John
disciple of the apostle John and by him ordained bishop of Smyrna was chief of all Asia
Irenæus' statement that he was appointed bishop of Smyrna by apostles is probably to be looked upon as a combination of his own.
But of this connexion with the Apostles, and especially with S. John, our biographer in the extant portion of the story says not a word.

myths.text: He was tied to a stake and the fire was lit. But the account says the fire would not burn him. It arched round him “like the sail of a ship when filled with the wind”. So an executioner stabbed him with a dagger. Only then was his body burned. Jerome's short notice, and many pages since, say simply “he was burned”.
myths.source: Martyrdom of Polycarp, chapters 15, 16 and 18; Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 17
myths.note: Eusebius's text agrees (Church History 4.15: 'commanded an executioner to approach and pierce him with the sword'). The Greek word is 'confector', the man who finished off wounded beasts in the arena (McGiffert note 1157). Catholic Online: 'The Romans burned him alive with twelve companions.'
evidence: At length, when those wicked men perceived that his body could not be consumed by the fire, they commanded an executioner to go near and pierce him through with a dagger.
The centurion then, seeing the strife excited by the Jews, placed the body in the midst of the fire, and consumed it.

myths.claim: “A dove flew out of his body.”
myths.text: So say all our Greek manuscripts: “there came forth a dove, and a great quantity of blood”. But Eusebius, who copied the chapter in the early 300s, has only the blood. Many think the dove is a copyist's slip. One old guess reads “on the left side” for “a dove”, a small change in Greek. Lightfoot thought the author of the fourth-century Life added it.
myths.source: Martyrdom of Polycarp, chapter 16, with ANF note 462; Eusebius, Church History 4.15, with McGiffert's note 1158; Lightfoot, Apostolic Fathers, Part II, vol. 1 (1889), p. 643
myths.note: Told as the text tells it in the miracles section; the doubt goes in 'Doubted from the start' in the sources' own words. Catholic Encyclopedia (1911): 'probably arose out of a textual corruption ... may also have been an interpolation by the pseudo-Pionius'.
evidence: there came forth a dove, and a great quantity of blood, so that the fire was extinguished
Eusebius omits all mention of the dove, and many have thought the text to be here corrupt. It has been proposed to read ep' aristera, "on the left hand side," instead of peristera, "a dove."
It seems probable that these words did not belong to the original text
this miracle appears only in the Pionian copies, not in Eusebius.
The story of the dove issuing from the body probably arose out of a textual corruption.

myths.text: He was the twelfth martyr of Smyrna, counting some from Philadelphia. The others died before him in the same persecution, some by wild beasts, like Germanicus. He died alone in the stadium. The 1916 Roman Martyrology has “twelve others”, from a slip in some copies of Eusebius.
myths.correction_2026_09_26: McGiffert note 1163: 'The majority of the mss.' of Eusebius, and Rufinus, read twelve; he thinks 'the change crept in later'. He does not link it to the Martyrology. Page now says so.
myths.source: Martyrdom of Polycarp, chapters 3 and 19; McGiffert's note 1163 on Eusebius, Church History 4.15; Roman Martyrology (1916), 26 January

myths.claim: “He was martyred under Marcus Aurelius, about 166.”
myths.text: That is Eusebius's date, and Jerome's after him. The letter itself names the governor, Statius Quadratus. In 1867 W. H. Waddington worked out from an orator's diary of illnesses (Aelius Aristides) when Quadratus governed Asia. The answer was 155 or 156, under Antoninus Pius. Most scholars have followed since.
myths.source: Martyrdom of Polycarp, chapter 21; McGiffert's note 1132 on Eusebius, Church History 4.15; Catholic Encyclopedia (1911), 'St. Polycarp'
myths.note: See hard_topics.date for both sides. The 1916 Roman Martyrology still gives 'under Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus' (Jerome's reign).
evidence: Polycarp's martyrdom occurred in Smyrna, not during the reign of Marcus Aurelius, as Eusebius says, but during the reign of Antoninus Pius, between 154 and 156 (probably in 155).
Afterwards during the reign of Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus
Now there are two possible years for this, 155 and 166.

facts.text: The account blames particular people in one crowd, on one day. It never speaks of the Jewish people as a whole. The same crowd was mostly pagan, shouting for their gods ('the overthrower of our gods').
facts.note: Our reading of the text; each phrase is in the evidence.
evidence: both of the heathen and Jews, who dwelt at Smyrna

holders_voice.text: The earlier scholars took the account at its word. Lightfoot (1889) explained the Jews' presence by the day. It was 'a great Sabbath', perhaps a feast, as at the martyrdom of Pionius in Smyrna in 250.
holders_voice.source: J. B. Lightfoot, The Apostolic Fathers, Part II, vol. 1 (1889), p. 471; vol. 3, note on chapter 12
holders_voice.note: Quotable (public domain): 'then, as now, the Jews were keeping holiday and busied themselves actively in the persecution, their fanatical zeal (we may suppose) being fanned by the associations of their own religious festival.' And (vol. 3): 'As in the Apostolic times, so also in subsequent ages, the Jews took an active part in instigating the persecutions of the Christians'. Both OCR, hyphens joined.
evidence: then, as now, the Jews were keeping holiday and busied themselves actively in the persecution, their fanatical zeal (we may suppose)
the Jews took an active part in instigating the persecutions of the Christians

holders_voice.text: McGiffert (1890), Eusebius's translator: 'The Jews appear very frequently as leading spirits in the persecution of Christians.' He pointed to Tertullian, who called the synagogues 'fountains of persecution'.
holders_voice.source: McGiffert, note 1151 on Eusebius, Church History 4.15
holders_voice.note: Tertullian's phrase ('synagogas Judaeorum, fontes persecutionum', Scorpiace 10) is quoted in Lightfoot's note.
evidence: The Jews appear very frequently as leading spirits in the persecution of Christians.

critics_voice.correction_2026_09_26: The source names one scholar's argument (Lloyd Gaston, 'highly unlikely'); page now says 'Some scholars'.
critics_voice.text: Many scholars now doubt that these details are history. The letter says it wants to show 'a martyrdom becoming the Gospel'. So it shapes Polycarp's death on Christ's: a Friday, a police chief named Herod, a traitor from his own house, a ride on an ass, a crowd shouting for death. The Jews in the crowd echo the Gospel crowds.
critics_voice.source: Judaism and Rome project (ERC, CNRS), commentary on the Martyrdom of Polycarp, drawing on Lloyd Gaston, 'Jewish Communities in Sardis and Smyrna'
critics_voice.note: One-sentence quote allowed (free web page): 'it is highly unlikely that the Jews’ behaviour described in Polycarp’s martyrdom narrative bears any historical credence'. The project dates the text 155-160 and calls Polycarp 'the eighty-six-year-old bishop' (see myths).
evidence: it is highly unlikely that the Jews’ behaviour described in Polycarp’s martyrdom narrative bears any historical credence
the Jews are simply added to the crowd alongside the Gentiles in order to create a further imitation of Christ’s passion
that the Lord might show us from above a martyrdom becoming the Gospel

the_jews_of_smyrna.note: Suggested plain wording: state the four lines as the letter says them; say Eusebius kept them; give Lightfoot's reading (a feast day, a real hostility) and the modern doubt (patterned on the Passion; Gaston). No verdict in our voice beyond 'scholars disagree whether this is history or a Gospel echo'. Do not generalise to 'the Jews' as a people.

facts.text: the blessed Polycarp suffered martyrdom on the second day of the month Xanthicus just begun, the seventh day before the Kalends of May, on the great Sabbath, at the eighth hour.
facts.display: the blessed Polycarp suffered martyrdom on the second day of the month Xanthicus just begun, the seventh day before the Kalends of May, on the great Sabbath, at the eighth hour.
facts.exact: the blessed Polycarp suffered martyrdom on the second day of the month Xanthicus just begun, the seventh day before the Kalends of May, on the great Sabbath, at the eighth hour.
facts.source: Martyrdom of Polycarp (the letter of the church at Smyrna), chapter 21, tr. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885)
facts.note: CAUTION: ANF's text says 'Kalends of May' (25 April). The Greek of Lightfoot and Lake says March: 'πρὸ ἑπτὰ καλανδῶν Μαρτίων', i.e. 23 February. Lightfoot translates 'the seventh before the kalends of March'. So quote Lightfoot for the date, or note ANF's reading. ANF note 477: 'Great obscurity hangs over the chronology here indicated.'
evidence: on the seventh before the kalends of March, on a great sabbath, at the eighth hour
Great obscurity hangs over the chronology here indicated.

facts.text: The letter names the governor, Statius Quadratus, and 'Philip the Trallian' as high priest. That is what lets the year be worked out.
facts.source: Martyrdom of Polycarp (the letter of the church at Smyrna), chapter 21, tr. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885)
evidence: Philip the Trallian being high priest, Statius Quadratus being proconsul, but Jesus Christ being King for ever

holders_voice.text: 155 or 156, under Antoninus Pius. W. H. Waddington (1867) dated Quadratus's year in Asia from the orator Aelius Aristides. Lightfoot defended it at length, and most scholars follow. 23 February 155 fell on a Saturday.
holders_voice.source: McGiffert, note 1132 on Eusebius, Church History 4.15; Catholic Encyclopedia (1911), 'St. Polycarp'; Lightfoot, Apostolic Fathers, Part II, vol. 1 (1889), pp. 646-677
holders_voice.note: CE 1911 adds new inscriptions (1904, 1906) that ruled out the rival system of Schmid.
evidence: This has been proved by Waddington
the martyrdom took place on a Saturday which fell on 23 February
Schmid's system, therefore, disappears, and Waddington's, in spite of some very real difficulties

critics_voice.text: Eusebius put it under Marcus Aurelius (his Chronicle: about 166-167), and Jerome followed. In the 1870s Wieseler and Keim argued again for 167. Lightfoot thought Eusebius meant only 'in the reign' and confused the emperors named Antoninus.
critics_voice.source: McGiffert, note 1132; Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 17
evidence: But the Chron. of Eusebius seems to put the martyrdom in the seventh year of Marcus Aurelius (166-167 a.d.)
Wieseler (in his Christenverfolgungen, 1878, p. 34-87) and Keim

critics_voice.text: And the text itself? Some scholars date the letter we have much later than the death. Candida Moss (2010) argued for the third century. Bart Ehrman (2013) agrees it was written 'at least some fifty years later', as if by eyewitnesses. Their reasons: the honour paid to the bones, the concern about volunteers (Quintus), and the postscript's tale of a lost copy found by revelation.
critics_voice.source: Bart D. Ehrman, Forgery and Counterforgery (2013), excerpt on his blog; Peter Kirby, 'Dating the Martyrdom of Polycarp in the Third Century'
critics_voice.note: Moss's article: Candida R. Moss, 'On the Dating of Polycarp: Rethinking the Place of the Martyrdom of Polycarp in the History of Christianity', Early Christianity 1 (2010) 539-574 (not fetched: paywalled; cited as Ehrman cites it). Kirby himself thinks late second century is enough to explain the text.
evidence: It was written at least some fifty years later.
the practice of collecting and venerating the bodies of the martyrs is unparalleled in second-century Christian literature
which still is compatible with authorship at the hand of a contemporary to Polycarp

critics_voice.text: Against them, the older view: the letter reads as a real eyewitness account. Lake (1913): 'This obviously genuine and contemporary account'. Lightfoot: it 'contains nothing which ought to excite a suspicion of its authenticity'.
critics_voice.source: Kirsopp Lake, The Apostolic Fathers, vol. 2 (1913), introduction to the Martyrdom; Lightfoot, Apostolic Fathers, Part II, vol. 1 (1889)
critics_voice.note: This is the holders' voice for the text's date.
evidence: this document contains nothing which ought to excite a suspicion of its

facts.text: The text we have came down through the Pionian edition. Eusebius is the only independent witness older than it, and his copy is shorter in places.
facts.source: Lightfoot, Apostolic Fathers, Part II, vol. 1 (1889), p. 643
evidence: Eusebius alone of all extant authorities is prior to the false Pionius and gives an independent text.

facts.text: The dove (chapter 16): in our manuscripts, not in Eusebius. See myths.
facts.source: ANF note 462; McGiffert note 1158; Lightfoot p. 643
evidence: Eusebius omits all mention of the dove

facts.text: A clause in chapter 17, 'the blameless one for sinners', is missing from Eusebius and may be a copyist's addition from 1 Peter 3:18.
evidence: This clause is omitted by Eusebius: it was probably interpolated by some transcriber, who had in his mind 1 Pet. iii. 18.

facts.text: The postscript (chapter 22) on Gaius, Socrates and Pionius is not part of the original letter. Lightfoot thought the author of the fourth-century Life wrote it, and that 'our spurious Pionius was before all things a miracle-monger'.
facts.source: ANF note 480; Lightfoot, Apostolic Fathers, Part II, vol. 1 (1889), p. 643
evidence: What follows is, of course, no part of the original Epistle.
Now our spurious Pionius was before all things a miracle-monger.

facts.text: The ANF editor (1885): 'That this Epistle has been interpolated can hardly be doubted, when we compare it with the unvarnished specimen, in Eusebius.' The older ANF note: some of 'the most startling miraculous phenomena' are not in Eusebius.
facts.source: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, introductory note to the Martyrdom
evidence: That this Epistle has been interpolated can hardly be doubted, when we compare it with the unvarnished specimen, in Eusebius.
some of the most startling miraculous phenomena recorded in the text as it now stands, have no place in the narrative as given by that early historian of the Church.

facts.text: The echoes of the Passion (Herod, the Friday, 'as against a robber', the betrayers who 'undergo the punishment of Judas') are in Eusebius's text too. The letter says outright that it tells a martyrdom 'becoming the Gospel'. Critics read the echoes as shaping; defenders as the church seeing its bishop follow his Lord.
facts.source: Martyrdom of Polycarp, chapters 1, 6, 7; Eusebius, Church History 4.15
facts.note: Eusebius 4.15 paraphrases chapters 5 to 7 (he tells the police captain's name, Herod, in section 15). The line 'the punishment of Judas' is not in Eusebius's text (he paraphrases that chapter).
evidence: that they who betrayed him might undergo the punishment of Judas himself
as if going out against a robber
And he was met by Herod, [1143] the captain of police

facts.text: The Moscow manuscript's longer ending adds Irenaeus in Rome hearing a trumpet-voice: a later addition (see myths).
evidence: The three preceding paragraphs as read in the Moscow MS.

later_additions.note: Lightfoot, though he thought the dove added, defended the rest: of the voice from heaven, 'the very simplicity of the narrative here disarms criticism' (vol. 1).
evidence_extra: simplicity of the narrative here disarms criticism

tidbits.text: His name is a Greek word meaning 'fruitful' or 'rich in fruit'.
The letter on his death is the oldest record of Christians keeping a martyr's death-day every year. They called it his 'birthday'.
tidbits.source: Martyrdom of Polycarp, chapter 18 (ANF note 470: literally 'the birth-day'); McGiffert, note 1162 on Eusebius 4.15
evidence: This is, so far as I am aware, the earliest notice of the annual celebration of the day of a martyr's death

tidbits.text: About a century later, in 250, the priest Pionius was arrested at Smyrna while keeping Polycarp's 'birthday'. He too was martyred.
tidbits.source: Lightfoot, Apostolic Fathers, Part II, vol. 1 (1889), p. 471, from the Acts of Pionius
evidence: were celebrating in Smyrna the ‘true birth-day of the martyr Polycarp,’ when they were apprehended and dragged to prison

tidbits.text: Ignatius's letters survive because Polycarp gathered them and sent copies to Philippi.
evidence: we have sent to you, as you requested

tidbits.text: The phrase 'the Catholic Church' is first found in a letter to his church: Ignatius's Letter to the Smyrnaeans.
tidbits.source: Ignatius, Letter to the Smyrnaeans, chapter 8; McGiffert, note 1136 on Eusebius 4.15
tidbits.note: Ignatius: 'wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the Catholic Church.' The Martyrdom uses the phrase four times.
evidence: wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the Catholic Church.
The phrase "Catholic Church" occurs first in Ignatius' Ep. ad Smyr., chap. 8

tidbits.text: Eusebius misread the letter's address. He thought it went to churches in Pontus, on the Black Sea. It went to Philomelium, in Phrygia.
tidbits.source: McGiffert, note 1134 on Eusebius, Church History 4.15
evidence: What led Eusebius to suppose that this epistle was addressed to the church in Pontus, we do not know.

tidbits.text: The Latin calendar long kept him on 26 January. His old day, 23 February, went to a different Polycarp, a Roman priest.
tidbits.source: Lightfoot, Apostolic Fathers, Part II, vol. 1 (1889), p. 471; Roman Martyrology (1916), index
tidbits.note: For the feasts researcher: the 1969 reform moved the Catholic memorial to 23 February (check against the calendar files).
evidence: In the Latin Calendar the day is January 26
February 23 is assigned to another Polycarp, a Roman presbyter and confessor

tidbits.text: In 1673 Heinrich Biber wrote a 'Sonata Sancti Polycarpi' for eight trumpets and drums. It was probably for a Salzburg churchman named after him, Polykarp von Khüenburg.
tidbits.source: McNaughtan Publishing, notes to Biber's Sonata Sancti Polycarpi
tidbits.note: The OCA Life says it was written 'in honor of the holy martyr'; the publisher's note gives the likely occasion. Modern secondary source; use only if a light tidbit is wanted.
evidence: The Archbishop of Salzburg's nephew was named Polykarp von Khüenburg.

tidbits.text: Eusebius dated a later Smyrna martyr, Pionius (died 250), to Polycarp's time, because the two accounts sat side by side in his book.
tidbits.source: McGiffert, note 1164 on Eusebius, Church History 4.15
evidence: But Eusebius has fallen into a serious chronological blunder in making these other martyrs contemporaries of Polycarp.

could_not_verify: Candida Moss, 'On the Dating of Polycarp' (Early Christianity 1, 2010): not fetched (paywalled). Cited only as Ehrman and Kirby report it. The German abstract file moss-2010-abstract-de.txt was fetched by another researcher; not read here.
Lloyd Gaston, 'Jewish Communities in Sardis and Smyrna' (in Religious Rivalries, 2006): not fetched; cited through the Judaism and Rome commentary only.

The origin of the patronage 'against earache and dysentery': not found in any source checked (1916 Martyrology, Catholic Encyclopedia, Lightfoot). Only modern sites (Catholic Online, Britannica FAQ) assert it.

'Everything we encounter today is used by God to prepare us for tomorrow...': a search engine summary listed it as a Polycarp quote, but the only page found is the Goodreads quote page of Rick Lambert's novel 'Polycarp, a destroyer of our gods' (quotes-goodreads-lambert-novel.txt). Not seen credited to Polycarp on a quote site; not used as a myth.
Latimer's 'play the man' at Oxford in 1555 as an echo of the voice to Polycarp: the wording matches, but no source found that says Latimer meant it; not used.

Lightfoot's full sentence 'Is it not the same dove ... let fly by the same hand?' runs across a page break in the OCR (vol. 1, pp. 643-644); only its first half is in the file. Peter Kirby's page quotes it whole. Use the verified shorter lines instead.

Whether the 'John' Polycarp heard was John the apostle or 'John the Elder': Irenaeus plainly means the apostle; Eusebius (Church History 3.39) showed Irenaeus could run the two Johns together in Papias's case. No free, citable modern discussion specific to Polycarp was fetched; left out of the myths.
